<font size=3 face="Verdana, Helvetica" color="#ffffff"><b>Harmless Algorithms - <font size=1>Issue 01 - Fine Occlusion Culling Algorithms</font></b><br>
<font size=2>by <a href="mailto:n/a">Edward Kmett</a> (09 April 1999)</font>
</font>
<br><br><br>
</td>

<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Introduction
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

The first thing that I want to discuss are the various forms of 
fine occlusion culling algorithms out there. Fine occlusion culling
is the process of separating actually visible polygons from
a predetermined potentially visible set. These algorithms do not
generally offer any order of magnitude speed increase to an average 
engine in and of themselves, however some of them do provide tools
useful to more general algorithms and visibility structures. <br><br>I am assuming at this point that the reader is at least generally 
familiar with a BSP tree's sorting properties, what a portal is, 
and is capable of rasterizing their own polygons or of using a 3d
hardware API such as Glide, OpenGL or Direct3d. I also assume at 
least passing familiarity with linked lists, binary trees, and 
other conventional data structures and algorithms.<br><br>The use of floats throughout here is intentional for subpixel accuracy
and ease of reading, if you prefer fixed points so be it.<br><br>The algorithms that will be covered here are the following:
<blockquote>
<li><A HREF=#sbuffer>S-Buffers</A>
<li><A HREF=#bst>Binary Span Trees (BST)</A>
<li><A HREF=#cbuffer>C-Buffers</A>
<li><A HREF=#ael>Active Edge Lists (AEL)</A>
<li><A HREF=#aeh>Active Edge Heaps</A>
<li><A HREF=#triage>Triage Masks</A>
<li><A HREF=#beamtrees>Beam Trees</A> 
</blockquote>
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

S-Buffers
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="sbuffer">
The s-buffer algorithm is described in Paul Nettle's s-buffer FAQ, 
and is a good starting place for looking at fine occlusion culling.<br><br>A classic s-buffer span-converts a polygon into a list of line 
segments. You have 1 bucket per scanline, and in that scanline you 
maintain a structures or class for an individual span which 
generally looks like:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> classic_sbuffer_span {
             <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_x;
             <font color="#0000ff">float</font> end_x;
             <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_ooz; <font color="#007f00">// 1/z, d(1/z)/dx
</font>
             ...              <font color="#007f00">// gradient setup for u and v, etc
</font>
             classic_sbuffer_poly * poly;
             classic_sbuffer_span * next;
       };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  In your poly object you contain information that is invariant over
  the entire poly (i.e. d(1/z)/dx, d(1/z)/dy) and as you insert spans
  into the buffer you clip against existing spans. How this is done
  depends on whether or not you can depend on the polygons going into
  the sbuffer to be sorted or not. <br><br>  <i><font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99">Interpenetrating Version:</font></i>
  <blockquote>
    Given the truly general case, which would allow for interpenetrating 
    spans and spans being inserted out of order, your inner loop for 
    inserting a given span not only has to look for what spans your 
    introduced polygon overlaps, but whether the interpolated 1/z regions
    overlap, and if they do, if the intersection is on or off of the 
    existing span and the inserted span. The number of special cases you
    need to handle in your inner insertion loop can grow prohibitive. 
    Also since you can later occlude a polygon that seemed like it was
    going to be in front, you have to do all of your rendering in a 
    post process or you risk unnecessary overdraw.
  </blockquote>  <br><br>  <i><font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99">Non-Interpenetrating Version:</font></i>
  <blockquote>
    Given the slightly less general case of assuming that there are no
    interpenetrating while still inserting spans out of order, you can
    handle most static worlds. Your inner loop simplifies tremendously
    compared to the more general algorithm.
  </blockquote>  <br><br>  <i><font size=2 face="Verdana,Helvetica" color="#ffff99">Immediate Rendering Version:</font></i>
  <blockquote>
    Next option. Instead of storing the gradient information, or for that 
    matter any information about the polygon in a span other than its
    starting and ending x position, and its starting z and d(1/z)/dx, you can
    make the assumption that whatever is feeding you polygons is doing so
    in a 'roughly' front to back order. If this is the case you can render
    each span when you clip it. This greatly shrinks the size of the
    individual span structures (to less than the size of a Pentium cache 
    line) which can improve your performance quite significantly. Now you
    no longer have a second pass through a fairly large data structure, but
    you risk some overdraw in the case of an imperfectly sorted scene and
    software rendering. This algorithm also has the advantage that it 
    renders in a texture coherent fashion.
  </blockquote><br><br>This data structure looks more like:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
         <font color="#0000ff">class</font> immediate_sbuffer_span {
               <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_x;
               <font color="#0000ff">float</font> end_x;
               <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_ooz;
               <font color="#0000ff">float</font> doozdx;
               immediate_sbuffer_span * next;
         };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center>
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Binary Span Trees
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="bst">Tom Hammersley devised this algorithm and used to have a detailed 
  description and source code up on his now non-existant website. 
  The span tree is very similar to the classic binary search tree
  algorithm. <br><br>  The first assumption made is that all polygons will be coming to 
  this algorithm in presorted order as from a conventional BSP tree
  or a recursive portal engine. <br><br>  Now you can only handle input that comes in perfect front-to-back
  order. Certain portal algorithms and BSP key sorting can provide this,
  but generally they do not provide this for dynamic actors. This generally 
  means that dynamic objects have to be moved off into another stage of 
  the pipeline in order to use this algorithm. This is not necessarily a bad thing
  depending on the purpose for the engine in question.<br><br>  Dynamic objects would then need to be z-buffered in, or clipped and then 
  inserted into the BSP before this stage. For hardware, 
  inserting all of the objects which are in visible BSP nodes directly 
  into the zbuffer is generally the most expedient approach.<br><br>The fundamental change is switching to a binary tree based structure:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> bst_span {
             <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_x, end_x; 
             bst_span * next, * prev;
       };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  Insertions clip their way down the tree. If you are lucky, the tree
  may reduce the number of spans visited as you clip your node.<br><br>  Relative to the more general s-buffer algorithm above, its primary
  speed up comes from the assumption of front-to-back order reducing
  the amount of clipping, than from any gains made by the tree itself.<br><br>  The problems I see with this algorithm is that its really just not seeing
  the forest for the trees. (no pun intended) In general, the goal of
  this algorithm, that is,  the reduction of the number of spans visited during
  the clipping and display of a given span is valid, but I have found
  that in practice (for me) a simpler algorithm (the c-buffer algorithm
  which follows) gives better results.<br><br>  An additional trait that is important in several of these algorithms, 
  that this approach provides, is the ability to check if a polygon 
  silhouette would be visible (span convert the polygon as if you were 
  going to insert into the tree, quit when you get your first visible
  sub span). You can perform this operation on the s-buffer algorithms 
  above, but not without a great deal of z computations.
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

C-Buffers
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="cbuffer">What I dubbed a coverage buffer (c-buffer for short) is another
  constrained variant on the s-buffer algorithm. Again, like the
  Binary Span Tree we will make the assumption that you can get
  your polygons to this stage of the pipeline in BSP front-to-back
  order.<br><br>  Your span definition shrinks to:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
       <font color="#0000ff">class</font> cbuffer_span {
           <font color="#0000ff">float</font> start_x, end_x;
           cbuffer_span * next;
       };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>
  Then walk left to right through the linked list per scanline. As you walk 
  if you clip on an existing node, congeal with it by just lowering its 
  minimum x value or raising its maximum x value, if you are clipped on both  
  sides, remove the second node, and expand the first one to its end boundary    <br><br>
<center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
  Example 1               
    Poly to draw         -------------|XXXXXXXXXXXX|-----------  
    Existing Span        -----|XXXXXXXXXXXX|-------------------  
    Rendered portion     ------------------|XXXXXXX|-----------  
    New Span in cbuffer  -----|XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX|-----------  <br><br>  Example 2 
    Poly to draw         ---------|XXXXXXXXXXXX|---------------  
    Existing Spans       ------|XXXXX|------|XXXXXX|-----------  
    Rendered Portion     ------------|XXXXXX|------------------  
    New Span in cbuffer  ------|XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX|-----------  <br><br>  Example 3 
    Poly to draw         ---|XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX|---------------  
    Existing Spans       ------|XXXXX|------|XXXXXX|-----------  
    Rendered Portions    ---|XX|-----|XXXXXX|------------------  
    New Span in cbuffer  ---|XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX|-----------  
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  Notice that examples 2 and 3 actually reclaimed a span data structure   
  for use in later spans. As the screen fills up the coverage buffer,   
  this algorithm actually lowers the number of spans in circulation, thus improving 
  performance. The reason that it works is because with perfect front-to-back ordering,
  you do not care about the z information at all in the
  span buffer; you simply need to know the portions of the screen which have been  
  covered. You know by definition of a bsp tree that the portions  
  already rendered cannot be concealed by polygons further away in the tree.  
  Render the portions as you walk the span buffer, and clip your   
  polygon fragment. This way you do not need to retain any of the clipped   
  values in the span buffer because you have already rendered them and filled 
  in your z-buffer if you so choose.   <br><br>  Notice also that now there is no longer a correlation between the number    
  of spans and the call to the rasterization routine, yet you still retain a  
  single draw per pixel. When the scene is filled, you end up with a single 
  fragment per scanline. <br><br>  This algorithm also shares the desirable quick would-this-polygon-be-visible
  test as the Binary Span Tree above.<br><br>  A variant proposed by Chris Babcock: <br><br>  In practice it is better to start with one span per scanline, and redefine
  your spans to be areas where there are no polygons. In this case you start with
  one span and converge an empty list by eating away pieces of it.<br><br>  Here's the "is visible" test for this variant: <br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">  
            <font color="#0000ff">bool</font> test_visible(cbuffer_line & line,<font color="#0000ff">int</font> start_x,<font color="#0000ff">int</font> end_x) {
                 cbuffer_span *scan = line.spans;
                 <font color="#0000ff">while</font> (scan) {
                    <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (end_x &lt;  scan->start_x) <font color="#0000ff">return</font> <font color="#0000ff">false</font>;
                    <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (start_x &lt;= scan->end_x) <font color="#0000ff">return</font> <font color="#0000ff">true</font>;
                    scan = scan->next;
                 }
                 <font color="#0000ff">return</font> <font color="#0000ff">false</font>;
            }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center>
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Active Edge Lists (AEL)
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="ael">There are at least two very good descriptions of this algorithm floating around 
  in Michael Abrash's Black Book (I can't recall if it was in the earlier Zen of 
  Graphics Programming) and in Computer Graphics: Principles and Practice;
  because of this, I will just summarize the algorithm's relative strengths 
  and weaknesses. An AEL allows insertion of the polygons in any order, but 
  requires a two-pass walk since you have to build up the data structure and then 
  afterwards you walk across the screen in a scanline coherent order while drawing.<br><br>  Its strength resides in the fact that it scales better to higher resolutions 
  than most of the algorithms above for software. Just like the first arbitrary 
  order s-Buffer variants above, you can throw any old polygon at it and this 
  stage of the pipeline will not choke.<br><br>  Unfortunately it renders in a scanline coherent manner, which generally causes a speed hit
  because almost all of your texture accesses are incoherent. Also, the two-stage
  rendering structure means you wind up building up the structure, having it go out
  of cache while you walk the scene and then have to walk through it all over again.<br><br>  Other concerns include that there are many data structures built up here, a linked list per
  scanline of edges that begin and end, a structure representing all of the 
  information needed to rasterize a given polygon, and then the sorted list of edges
  that you use as you walk across the scanline, and the small list of polygons that 
  overlap the current pixel. Each one unto themselves is fairly minor, but it does
  add significant complexity to an implementation.<br><br>  This algorithm does not possess a corollary to the visible polygon test, which means 
  that every potentially visible polygon needs to be inserted into the structure that
  is walked in the second stage. Depending on how conservative of a set your gross 
  culling and occlusion algorithm is this may or may not be a problem (Witness quake
  which uses this algorithm).
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Active Edge Heaps (AEH)
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="aeh">This is an algorithm I used briefly in a software rendering engine that I found 
  useful enough to relate. Its goal was to address the number of data structures
  floating around in the Active Edge Table algorithm above by using a binomial 
  heap.<br><br>  Like the AEL approach above, this algorithm does not require front to back sorting,
  nor does it even gain anything from it.<br><br>  For those not familiar with a binomial heap, I refer you to any of Robert Sedgewick's 
  books on Algorithms (or for that matter almost any Algorithm text). A binomial heap 
  is also known as a priority queue, and is used for the heap sort.<br><br>  A heap is a form of binary tree that is always packed in memory (which is very good 
  for cache coherence).  The basic change is to use either an xy pair or a screen coordinate as a key for a node 
  in the binomial heap.  Initialize each edge with the position along each edge at its top y
  coordinate.<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
      <font color="#0000ff">class</font> aeh_edge {
            <font color="#0000ff">int</font> type;  <font color="#007f00">// start or end of a span - 1 or -1.
</font>            <font color="#0000ff">float</font> x, ooz;
            <font color="#0000ff">int</font> y, last_y;
            <font color="#0000ff">float</font> dxdy, doozdx, doozdy;
            aeh_poly * poly;
      };
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  One property provided by a binomial heap is the ability to quickly extract the entry 
  with the highest priority (or lowest key). Using the key as the current xy value of a 
  given entry, you will automatically start on the top scanline with the beginning of the 
  first span by extracting the top node of the heap.<br><br>psuedo-code:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">  
         <font color="#0000ff">while</font> (heap isnt empty) {
             look at node at top of heap
                <font color="#0000ff">if</font> its the start of an edge add poly to the list of current spans. 
                <font color="#0000ff">else</font> remove poly from the list of current spans.<br><br>             increase y, <font color="#0000ff">if</font> its less than last_y then
                add dxdy and doozdy to the x and ooz values and reinsert (you can
                quickly reinsert the top node of a binomial heap by decreasing its
                priority and then verifying the heap sorting property.)<br><br>             draw from the coordinate stated to the node at the top of the heap.
         }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  There are fewer data structures than in the case of an AEL. You no longer have the separate
  buckets per scanline for insertion and deletion of nodes on each pass. The initial insertion 
  cost of each of the edges is higher than for an AEL and you are still stuck with a two-pass
  data structure. On the other hand, you aren't stuck iterating through the list of active 
  edges for every scanline to insert and delete each one that begins or ends on a given scanline. <br><br>  I present this algorithm as an example of the trade-offs involved in different approaches. This
  lacks a quick polygon visibility just test like the Active Edge Table method above unfortunately
  does.
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Triage Masks
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="triage">Ned Greene of Apple published a very interesting and <A HREF="http://www2.bloodshed.com/cgi-bin/pm.cgi?filename=greene96.ps&page=db" Target=_blank>often overlooked paper</A> on the subject 
  of a variant on Warnock's algorithm (quadtree subdivision of the view) that used what he 
  called triage masks. Rather than present his work here, I'll simply provide a <A HREF="http://www2.bloodshed.com/cgi-bin/pm.cgi?filename=greene96.ps&page=db" Target=_blank>pointer</A> to the 
  original document, a brief overview, and compare and contrast it with the other algorithms above.<br><br>  Triage mask are a hierarchial form of coverage buffering that uses binary bit operations to 
  check for occlusion or probable occlusion. In his paper, Ned Greene used 8x8 masks which required
  64 bit binary operations. The intersection or union of 3 or more masks provides the silhouette 
  at a given depth of this hierarchial occlusion structure. In short the triage mask data structure 
  enables you to quickly evaluate if a polygon is visible or not with a few binary operations, 
  and if the resolution of that query is insufficient to find out what subcels you need to zoom in
  on and evaluate to determine whether or not the polygon is visible.<br><br>  The requirements are the same as for the Binary Span Tree and for the C-Buffer: Perfect
  front to back presorting.<br><br>  The good part of this algorithm is that as your scene fills up you can quickly reject whole 
  polygons with a handful of binary operations.<br><br>  Problems include that the preprocess of generating the masks is easy to mess up and I haven't 
  yet found a way to do the edge of cel intersections as fast as I'd like to. Scaling up in
  multiples of 8x8 is somewhat scary, given your virtual screen resolutions for this go from
  8x8 to 64x64 to 512x512 to 4096x4096, and while that is reassuring for future video resolutions, 
  under 1024x768 or so this algorithm seems to be, for me, a net loss. <br><br>  This algorithm supplies a very good spot checked polygon visibility test.
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Beam Trees
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

<a name="beamtrees">Unlike the rest of the algorithms above, this algorithm takes place in object space.
  This means that you can get away cheaper on the polygons that you do not display. 
  Another concern not addressed by the methods above is the matter of subpixel accuracy 
  and conservative estimation. This algorithm is also applicable for shadow casting 
  light sources, but that is another topic for another day.<br><br>  A beamtree, as I describe herein, should really be thought of as a 3
  dimensional structure. It really is just a specialized form of BSP tree.
  In a beamtree all planes pass through the origin (the eye point).
  Other than that it subdivides the view as you walk from front to back
  through the scene into drawn and undrawn sections, much like a solid
  BSP can divide between solid portions of the map and air. Since all
  planes pass through the origin, their 'd' component is always 0, which
  means you do not need to normalize the planes during beamtree generation
  because when you use the distances from the plane for linear interpolation,
  the magnitude of the plane 'normal' is irrelevant and cancels itself out.<br><br>  In short, the plane passing through two points in the scene and the origin is:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">plane' = (v1-eye) cross (v2-eye) </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>then to get the side of that plane any point is on:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">side = the sign of ((vertex-eye) . plane') </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  For a given viewpoint, the beamtree is used by putting in place 4 'slabs'
  representing the left, right, top and bottom of the viewing fustrum.<br><br>  This gives you a degenerate tree like:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">  
    left
   /    \
solid   right
        /    \
    solid    top
             /  \
         solid  bottom
                /    \
             solid   open
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  The above use of an arbitrary plane and its opposite is necessary, because 
  otherwise the first plane you inserted into the beamtree would cause half of 
  the field of view from the light source to fall into shadow. <br><br>  When you insert a polygon, you walk down the beamtree with all of the points in your
  polygon, visiting each side that the points lie on. <br><br>  You do not need to define the leaf nodes. Anything that opens to an empty 'left' 
  child is solid anything opening to an empty 'right' child is open and unrendered. so think 
  of left and right as 'drawn/undrawn' or vice versa.<br><br>  Your recursive insertion routine would look something like:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">
     <font color="#0000ff">#define</font> EPSILON 1.0e-6<br><br>     <font color="#0000ff">int</font> convervative_signof(<font color="#0000ff">float</font> value) {
          <font color="#0000ff">int</font> result;
          <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (value &lt; -EPSILON) <font color="#0000ff">return</font> 1;
          <font color="#0000ff">else</font> <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (value > EPSILON) <font color="#0000ff">return</font> 2;
          <font color="#0000ff">else</font> <font color="#0000ff">return</font> 0;
     }<br><br>     <font color="#0000ff">bool</font> recursive_insertion(vertex * fragment, <font color="#0000ff">int</font> nvertices, beamtree_node & node) {
          <font color="#0000ff">int</font> sign=0, * signs = (<font color="#0000ff">int</font> *)alloca(nvertices*<font color="#0000ff">sizeof</font>(<font color="#0000ff">int</font>));
          <font color="#0000ff">for</font> (<font color="#0000ff">int</font> i=0;i&lt;nvertices;++i) {
              sign |= signs[i] = conservative_signof (fragment[i] dot node.plane);
          }
          <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (sign == 1) {
              <font color="#007f00">// generally you just throw these away as terminating on a solid node.
</font>          } <font color="#0000ff">else</font> <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (sign == 2) {
              right_attach(fragment,nvertices,node);
          } <font color="#0000ff">else</font> <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (sign == 3) {
              <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (node->left) {<br><br>                  in here find the contiguous set of vertices that have a
                  conservative_signof of all 0's and 1's, passing along any
                  2's that precede or follow a beginning or final 1. <font color="#0000ff">this</font>
                  needs to wrap around to the beginning of the set as well.<br><br>                  recursive_insertion(the set, # of verts, *node->left);
             } <font color="#0000ff">else</font> {
                  <font color="#007f00">// throw it away as terminating on a solid node
</font>             }<br><br>             out here find the contiguous set of vertices that have a
             conservative_signof of all 0's and 2's, and along any 1's
             that precede or follow a beginning or final 2.<br><br>             <font color="#0000ff">if</font> (node->right) {
                 recursive_insertion(the set, # of verts, *node->right);
             } <font color="#0000ff">else</font> {
                 right_attach(the set, number of vertices in the set, node);
             }
          }
     }
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  right_attach takes the edges between the supplied vertices and inserts them as planes
  using the equation given on the right hand side of the current plane.<br><br>  In short, when you recurse to a solid node you throw away that fragment because its occluded.<br><br>  When you recurse to an open node, you take all edges of the polygon that have
  a point that has recursed this far and insert those edges as solid planes,
  the consistency of your clockwise or counterclockwise winding will orient the
  plane to maintain the proper sidedness relationship.<br><br>  Any polygon that requires you to modify the tree is visible.<br><br>  You can give the eye a 360 degree frustum with the following trickery:<br><br><center><div style="width:100%; overflow:auto; background-color:#FFFFFF; border:solid 1px #c0c0c0;"><table width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=12 border=0><tr><td width="100%" bgcolor="#ffffff"><pre><font face="Courier, Courier New" color="#000000">  
         plane
         /   \ 
      -plane  open
       /  \
   solid   open
 </font></pre></td></tr></table></div></center><br><br>  If you don't start with some arbitrary plane, the first plane being inserted at the root would
  occlude half the surfaces from the standpoint of the light. <br><br>  Relative to the rest of the algorithms above, this approach is least likely to run afoul
  of pixel sized gaps due to scan conversion problems.<br><br>  If you are looking for similar algorithms to compare with, this is very similar to Naylor's 
  algorithm for performing CSG with a BSP tree and a B-rep. <br><br>  This algorithm provides a polygon visibility test, its not as fast as the triage or cbuffer
  polygon visibility test, but it has the potential to avoid a lot of scan conversion problems
  that affect the other algorithms.<br><br>  I will be supplying tricks to collapse a beamtree in manners similar to the cbuffer algorithm,
  when I get around to talking about lighting.
</font></td></tr></table>
</center><br><br><center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=3 color="#ffffff" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman"><b>

Summary
<font size=1><br><img src="line_grey.png"><br><br></font></b></font></td></tr></table>
</center>
<center>
<table style="table-layout:fixed;" width="80%" cellspacing=0 cellpadding=0 border=0>
<tr>
<td width="100%">
<font size=2 color="#FFE291" face="Verdana, Helvetica, Arial, Times New Roman">

These algorithms do not in-and-of-themselves solve visibility problems; they are merely  
  ways to take polygons from a pretty good guess of what is visible and determine if they 
  are indeed visible. When combined with some on-the-fly gross culling/vis system they can 
  be used to build a viable engine. Next time I'll review some of the various visibility
  systems, which of these that they will work with, and the relative merits and flaws
  of each.<br><br>  Indeed all of the algorithms above can potentially run afoul of problems when
  used in conjunction with hardware; if your edge conversion doesn't exactly correspond with
  the algorithm used by the graphics card you may wind up with fragments of polygons that
  your algorithm says aren't visible. The beamtree avoids one stage in which this error
  usually crops up, but it doesn't shrink as polygons are added as does the cbuffer algorithm.<br><br>  Which of these you use (or if you use another) should probably be determined by what 
  gross culling and visibility determination algorithm you are using and whether or not you are
  writing for hardware, software, or a hybrid game engine.<br><br><i>Harmless</i><br>
April  8, 1999<br><br>You can contact the author at the following address: <a href="mailto:harmless@bloodshed.com">harmless@bloodshed.com</a><br><br>You can also check out his web site at: <a target="_blank" href="http://www.bloodshed.com">http://www.bloodshed.com</a><br><br><i><font size=1>This document is (C) 1999 Edward Kmett and may not be reproduced in any way without
explicit permission from the author (Edward Kmett).</font></i>
</font></td></tr></table>
